sentenceSets.sentence: She redoubled her efforts when the difficulty became apparent, treating the obstacle as evidence that the approach was worth pursuing.

answerChoices.reasoning: The sentence describes a surge of effort touched off by an unexpected obstacle, not a measured twofold increase that someone could have calculated in advance.

Plausible, but the sentence stresses that she was already working hard before the difficulty appeared, so what changed is the sheer quantity of effort piled on top of the existing effort rather than its concentration.
The sentence tracks one person pouring more of herself into a single approach, whereas this word suggests effort proliferating into many separate lines of work.
Nothing in the sentence says her work had lapsed or stopped; the obstacle appears while she is already engaged, so a word implying a restart misreads the timeline.
The sentence gives no interruption for her to pick up from, which is what this word requires.
The obstacle prompts more work rather than faster work; the sentence says nothing about pace or deadlines.
Merely holding effort steady would not match a response in which the difficulty itself is taken as a reason to invest more.
This implies narrowing her focus, but the sentence describes her committing further to the same approach, not selecting among competing ones.
She treats the obstacle as a reason to keep going, the opposite of giving up.
Cutting effort short contradicts the sentence's point that she judged the approach worth pursuing.
Easing off makes no sense when the sentence presents the difficulty as motivating rather than discouraging.

sentenceSets.sentence: After the storm cleared, rescuers redoubled their search of the flooded district, refusing to pause even as the second night set in.

answerChoices.reasoning: This word suits a conflict or dispute that grows more severe, while the sentence describes teams simply putting far more work into an ongoing search.
The sentence keeps the search fixed on one flooded district and emphasizes hours worked, not additional ground covered.
The detail that they refused to pause through a second night points to added labor and persistence rather than a faster tempo.
Hurrying conflicts with the picture of crews grinding on through the night; the sentence measures their response in endurance, not speed.
No new streets or zones are mentioned, so nothing in the sentence supports a change in the search's boundaries.
Working into a second night already shows duration, but the sentence frames this as a deliberate increase in the effort itself, not merely more time on the clock.
The sentence says nothing about organizing teams or agencies; it describes what the rescuers did after the weather broke.
The search is clearly already under way and never stops, so there is nothing to begin again.
The rescuers explicitly refuse to pause, which rules out stopping.
Putting the search off contradicts the clause about working through the second night.
The sentence is about labor in a flooded district, not about announcing anything to the public.

sentenceSets.sentence: Every attempt to shout him down only redoubled the senator's determination to read the entire report into the record.

answerChoices.reasoning: This suggests resolve becoming more rigid, whereas the sentence shows each interruption adding to an already firm determination.
Hardening implies a change in the character of his resolve, but the sentence tracks how much resolve the heckling produced, not what kind.
Close, yet the sentence's 'every attempt' sets up a cumulative piling-on rather than a single reinforcement.
This word usually describes making something appear larger, which sits oddly with a determination that is actually growing because of the heckling.
Propping up an existing conviction is weaker than what the sentence shows, where the opposition itself becomes fuel for more.
His determination predates the shouting, since he already intends to read the report, so it is not called into being by the interruptions.
Confirming would leave his resolve unchanged, but the sentence presents each attempt as making a difference to it.
The heckling in this sentence acts on the senator's own resolve, not on how widely his intentions were made known.
The word 'only' signals that the hecklers achieved the reverse of what they wanted.
His determination plainly survives, since he goes on reading the report into the record.
Nothing about being shouted down makes him more accommodating in this sentence.
